# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# grep_searcher - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/grep-searcher

## Expand description

This crate provides an implementation of line oriented search, with optional support for multi-line search.

[§](https://docs.rs#brief-overview)Brief overview

The principle type in this crate is a [ Searcher](https://docs.rs/struct.Searcher.html), which can be configured
and built by a

[. A](https://docs.rs/struct.SearcherBuilder.html)

`SearcherBuilder``Searcher` is responsible for reading
bytes from a source (e.g., a file), executing a search of those bytes using
a `Matcher` (e.g., a regex) and then reporting the results of that search to
a [(e.g., stdout). The](https://docs.rs/trait.Sink.html)

`Sink``Searcher` itself is principally responsible
for managing the consumption of bytes from a source and applying a `Matcher`
over those bytes in an efficient way. The `Searcher` is also responsible for
inverting a search, counting lines, reporting contextual lines, detecting
binary data and even deciding whether or not to use memory maps.A `Matcher` (which is defined in the
[ grep-matcher](https://crates.io/crates/grep-matcher) crate) is a trait
for describing the lowest levels of pattern search in a generic way. The
interface itself is very similar to the interface of a regular expression.
For example, the

[crate provides an implementation of the](https://crates.io/crates/grep-regex)

`grep-regex``Matcher` trait using Rust’s
[crate.](https://crates.io/crates/regex)

`regex`Finally, a `Sink` describes how callers receive search results producer by a
`Searcher`. This includes routines that are called at the beginning and end of
a search, in addition to routines that are called when matching or contextual
lines are found by the `Searcher`. Implementations of `Sink` can be trivially
simple, or extraordinarily complex, such as the `Standard` printer found in
the [ grep-printer](https://crates.io/crates/grep-printer) crate, which
effectively implements grep-like output. This crate also provides convenience

`Sink` implementations in the [sub-module for easy searching with closures.](https://docs.rs/sinks/index.html)

`sinks`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This example shows how to execute the searcher and read the search results
using the [ UTF8](https://docs.rs/sinks/struct.UTF8.html) implementation of

`Sink`.```
use {
    grep_matcher::Matcher,
    grep_regex::RegexMatcher,
    grep_searcher::Searcher,
    grep_searcher::sinks::UTF8,
};
const SHERLOCK: &'static [u8] = b"\
For the Doctor Watsons of this world, as opposed to the Sherlock
Holmeses, success in the province of detective work must always
be, to a very large extent, the result of luck. Sherlock Holmes
can extract a clew from a wisp of straw or a flake of cigar ash;
but Doctor Watson has to have it taken out for him and dusted,
and exhibited clearly, with a label attached.
";
let matcher = RegexMatcher::new(r"Doctor \w+")?;
let mut matches: Vec<(u64, String)> = vec![];
Searcher::new().search_slice(&matcher, SHERLOCK, UTF8(|lnum, line| {
    // We are guaranteed to find a match, so the unwrap is OK.
    let mymatch = matcher.find(line.as_bytes())?.unwrap();
    matches.push((lnum, line[mymatch].to_string()));
    Ok(true)
}))?;
assert_eq!(matches.len(), 2);
assert_eq!(
    matches[0],
    (1, "Doctor Watsons".to_string())
);
assert_eq!(
    matches[1],
    (5, "Doctor Watson".to_string())
);
```
See also `examples/search-stdin.rs` from the root of this crate’s directory
to see a similar example that accepts a pattern on the command line and
searches stdin.

# delta_funnel - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/delta-funnel/0.1.3/delta_funnel/

## Expand description

Core library for Delta Funnel.

This crate will own the high-level export orchestration from table formats
such as Delta Lake into Microsoft SQL Server. Low-level Arrow to TDS bulk
loading is expected to stay in `arrow-tiberius`.

Module boundaries should follow the load workflow. `table_formats` owns
upstream table-format integrations, starting with Delta source configuration
and snapshot loading. Later DataFusion provider, query execution, SQL Server
sink, and orchestration work should land in their own modules when the first
real implementation slice needs them.

# shikumi - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/shikumi/0.1.128/shikumi/

## Expand description

Shikumi (仕組み) — config discovery, hot-reload, and `ArcSwap` store
for Nix-managed desktop applications.

Extracted from [karakuri](https://github.com/pleme-io/karakuri)’s configuration
system, shikumi provides the shared infrastructure for desktop apps that need:

- **XDG config discovery**with env var overrides and format preference
- **Figment provider chains**(defaults → env vars → config file)
- **Lock-free concurrent reads**via- `ArcSwap`
- **Hot-reload**with symlink-aware file watching (for nix-darwin managed configs)

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use serde::Deserialize;
use shikumi::{ConfigDiscovery, ConfigStore, Format};
#[derive(Deserialize, Clone, Debug, Default)]
struct MyConfig {
    window_width: Option<u32>,
}
let path = ConfigDiscovery::new("myapp")
    .env_override("MYAPP_CONFIG")
    .formats(&[Format::Yaml, Format::Toml])
    .discover()
    .expect("config file not found");
let store = ConfigStore::<MyConfig>::load(&path, "MYAPP_")
    .expect("failed to load config");
let config = store.get();
println!("width: {:?}", config.window_width);
```

# yew_nav_link - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/yew-nav-link/0.10.7/yew_nav_link/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#yew-nav-link)yew-nav-link

Navigation link component for [Yew](https://yew.rs) with automatic active
state detection.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

`yew-nav-link` provides a [ NavLink](https://docs.rs/active_link/nav_link/struct.NavLink.html) component that wraps Yew Router’s

`Link` with automatic active state management. When the target route matches
the current URL, an `active` CSS class is applied.[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
[dependencies]
yew-nav-link = "0.10"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#component-syntax)Component Syntax

```
use yew::prelude::*;
use yew_nav_link::NavLink;
use yew_router::prelude::*;
#[derive(Clone, PartialEq, Debug, Routable)]
enum Route {
    #[at("/")]
    Home,
    #[at("/about")]
    About
}
#[component]
fn Navigation() -> Html {
    html! {
        <nav>
            <NavLink<Route> to={Route::Home}>{ "Home" }</NavLink<Route>>
            <NavLink<Route> to={Route::About}>{ "About" }</NavLink<Route>>
        </nav>
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#function-syntax)Function Syntax

For text-only links, use [ nav_link()](https://docs.rs/active_link/nav_link/fn.nav_link.html) with explicit

[mode:](https://docs.rs/active_link/mode/enum.Match.html)

`Match````
use yew::prelude::*;
use yew_nav_link::{Match, nav_link};
use yew_router::prelude::*;
#[component]
fn Menu() -> Html {
    html! {
        <nav>
            { nav_link(Route::Home, "Home", Match::Exact) }
            { nav_link(Route::Docs, "Docs", Match::Partial) }
        </nav>
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#partial-matching)Partial Matching

Use `partial` prop to keep parent links active on nested routes:

```
use yew::prelude::*;
use yew_nav_link::NavLink;
use yew_router::prelude::*;
#[component]
fn Navigation() -> Html {
    html! {
        <nav>
            // Active on /docs, /docs/api, /docs/*
            <NavLink<Route> to={Route::Docs} partial=true>{ "Docs" }</NavLink<Route>>
        </nav>
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#css-classes)CSS Classes

| Class | Condition |
|---|---|
| `nav-link` | Always |
| `active` | Route matches |

Compatible with Bootstrap, Tailwind, and other CSS frameworks.

[§](https://docs.rs#requirements)Requirements

- Yew 0.23+
- yew-router 0.20+

# sim_lib_skill - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-skill/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_skill/

## Expand description

Agent skills for the SIM runtime.

A *skill* is a callable capability that an agent can invoke – a tool, a
model, a resource, a prompt, a memory, a retriever, a judge, or a router.
Each skill is described by a [ SkillCard](https://docs.rs/struct.SkillCard.html) that pairs a stable identity and
symbol with input and output

[contracts, a](https://docs.rs/sim-shape/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_shape/index.html)

`sim_shape`[governing caching/recording/privacy, and the transport that actually runs the call. Cards are bound into a](https://docs.rs/struct.SkillPolicy.html)

`SkillPolicy`[and exposed as ordinary callable runtime objects through](https://docs.rs/struct.SkillRegistry.html)

`SkillRegistry`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.SkillCallable.html)

`SkillCallable`Behavior is provided by a [ SkillTransport](https://docs.rs/trait.SkillTransport.html): a backend (fixture, HTTP, MCP,
process, OpenAI-compatible server, …) that knows how to discover and call
skills.

[registers the](https://docs.rs/struct.SkillLib.html)

`SkillLib``skill/*` operations (install, bind,
list, card, call, and the feature-gated audit/tool/runner/serve surfaces)
when the library is loaded into a [.](https://docs.rs/sim-kernel/0.1.0-rc.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sim_kernel/env/core/struct.Cx.html)

`sim_kernel::Cx`Optional Cargo features select transports and integrations: `mcp`, `http`,
`openai`, `process`, `agent`, `runner`, `serve`, and the `cache`/`cassette`
recording surfaces.

# noslop - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/noslop/0.2.0/noslop/

## Expand description

noslop - Pre-commit checks with acknowledgment tracking

This library provides the core functionality for:

- Defining checks that must be reviewed when code changes
- Tracking acknowledgments that prove review happened
- Integrating with git hooks for enforcement

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

The library follows a hexagonal (ports & adapters) architecture:

-
`core`- `core::models`
- `core::ports`
- `core::services`

-
`adapters`- `adapters::toml`

# cumulus_client_pov_recovery - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cumulus-client-pov-recovery/0.32.0/cumulus_client_pov_recovery/

## Expand description

Parachain PoV recovery

A parachain needs to build PoVs that are send to the relay chain to progress. These PoVs are erasure encoded and one piece of it is stored by each relay chain validator. As the relay chain decides on which PoV per parachain to include and thus, to progress the parachain it can happen that the block corresponding to this PoV isn’t propagated in the parachain network. This can have several reasons, either a malicious collator that managed to include its own PoV and doesn’t want to share it with the rest of the network or maybe a collator went down before it could distribute the block in the network. When something like this happens we can use the PoV recovery algorithm implemented in this crate to recover a PoV and to propagate it with the rest of the network.

It works in the following way:

-
For every included relay chain block we note the backed candidate of our parachain. If the block belonging to the PoV is already known, we do nothing. Otherwise we start a timer that waits for a randomized time inside a specified interval before starting to recover the PoV.
-
If between starting and firing the timer the block is imported, we skip the recovery of the PoV.
-
If the timer fired we recover the PoV using the relay chain PoV recovery protocol.

4a. After it is recovered, we restore the block and import it.

4b. Since we are trying to recover pending candidates, availability is not guaranteed. If the block PoV is not yet available, we retry.

If we need to recover multiple PoV blocks (which should hopefully not happen in real life), we make sure that the blocks are imported in the correct order.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [PoVRecovery](https://docs.rs/struct.PoVRecovery.html)
- Encapsulates the logic of the pov recovery.
- [Recovery](https://docs.rs/struct.RecoveryDelayRange.html)- Delay - Range
- The delay between observing an unknown block and triggering the recovery of a block. Randomizing the start of the recovery within this interval can be used to prevent self-DOSing if the recovery request is part of a distributed protocol and there is the possibility that multiple actors are requiring to perform the recovery action at approximately the same time.
- [Recovery](https://docs.rs/struct.RecoveryRequest.html)- Request
- Structure used to trigger an explicit recovery request via `PoVRecovery`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Recovery](https://docs.rs/enum.RecoveryKind.html)- Kind
- Type of recovery to trigger.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Recovery](https://docs.rs/trait.RecoveryHandle.html)- Handle
- Test-friendly wrapper trait for the overseer handle. Can be used to simulate failing recovery requests.

# grep-matcher 0.1.8 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/grep-matcher/0.1.8

## grep-matcher

This crate provides a low level interface for describing regular expression
matchers. The `grep` crate uses this interface in order to make the regex
engine it uses pluggable.

Dual-licensed under MIT or the [UNLICENSE](https://unlicense.org/).

### Documentation

**NOTE:** You probably don't want to use this crate directly. Instead, you
should prefer the facade defined in the
[ grep](https://docs.rs/grep)
crate.

### Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.1"
```

# grep_matcher - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/grep-matcher/0.1.8/target-redirect/grep_matcher/

## Expand description

This crate provides an interface for regular expressions, with a focus on line
oriented search. The purpose of this crate is to provide a low level matching
interface that permits any kind of substring or regex implementation to power
the search routines provided by the
[ grep-searcher](https://docs.rs/grep-searcher)
crate.

The primary thing provided by this crate is the [ Matcher](https://docs.rs/trait.Matcher.html) trait. The trait
defines an abstract interface for text search. It is robust enough to support
everything from basic substring search all the way to arbitrarily complex
regular expression implementations without sacrificing performance.

A key design decision made in this crate is the use of *internal iteration*,
or otherwise known as the “push” model of searching. In this paradigm,
implementations of the `Matcher` trait will drive search and execute callbacks
provided by the caller when a match is found. This is in contrast to the
usual style of *external iteration* (the “pull” model) found throughout the
Rust ecosystem. There are two primary reasons why internal iteration was
chosen:

- Some search implementations may themselves require internal iteration. Converting an internal iterator to an external iterator can be non-trivial and sometimes even practically impossible.
- Rust’s type system isn’t quite expressive enough to write a generic interface using external iteration without giving something else up (namely, ease of use and/or performance).

In other words, internal iteration was chosen because it is the lowest common denominator and because it is probably the least bad way of expressing the interface in today’s Rust. As a result, this trait isn’t specifically intended for everyday use, although, you might find it to be a happy price to pay if you want to write code that is generic over multiple different regex implementations.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [ByteSet](https://docs.rs/struct.ByteSet.html)
- A set of bytes.
- [Line](https://docs.rs/struct.LineTerminator.html)- Terminator
- A line terminator.
- [Match](https://docs.rs/struct.Match.html)
- The type of a match.
- [NoCaptures](https://docs.rs/struct.NoCaptures.html)
- NoCaptures provides an always-empty implementation of the `Captures`trait.
- [NoError](https://docs.rs/struct.NoError.html)
- NoError provides an error type for matchers that never produce errors.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Line](https://docs.rs/enum.LineMatchKind.html)- Match - Kind
- The type of match for a line oriented matcher.

[43](https://docs.rs#43)/// The type of a match.
[44](https://docs.rs#44)///
[45](https://docs.rs#45)/// The type of a match is a possibly empty range pointing to a contiguous
[46](https://docs.rs#46)/// block of addressable memory.
[47](https://docs.rs#47)///
[48](https://docs.rs#48)/// Every `Match` is guaranteed to satisfy the invariant that `start <= end`.
[49](https://docs.rs#49)///
[50](https://docs.rs#50)/// # Indexing
[51](https://docs.rs#51)///
[52](https://docs.rs#52)/// This type is structurally identical to `std::ops::Range<usize>`, but
[53](https://docs.rs#53)/// is a bit more ergonomic for dealing with match indices. In particular,
[54](https://docs.rs#54)/// this type implements `Copy` and provides methods for building new `Match`
[55](https://docs.rs#55)/// values based on old `Match` values. Finally, the invariant that `start`
[56](https://docs.rs#56)/// is always less than or equal to `end` is enforced.
[57](https://docs.rs#57)///
[58](https://docs.rs#58)/// A `Match` can be used to slice a `&[u8]`, `&mut [u8]` or `&str` using
[59](https://docs.rs#59)/// range notation. e.g.,
[60](https://docs.rs#60)///
[61](https://docs.rs#61)/// ```
[62](https://docs.rs#62)/// use grep_matcher::Match;
[63](https://docs.rs#63)///
[64](https://docs.rs#64)/// let m = Match::new(2, 5);
[65](https://docs.rs#65)/// let bytes = b"abcdefghi";
[66](https://docs.rs#66)/// assert_eq!(b"cde", &bytes[m]);
[67](https://docs.rs#67)/// ```
[68](https://docs.rs#68)#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Eq, Hash, PartialEq)]
[69](https://docs.rs#69)pub struct Match {
[70](https://docs.rs#70)    start: usize,
[71](https://docs.rs#71)    end: usize,
[72](https://docs.rs#72)}

[183](https://docs.rs#183)/// A line terminator.
[184](https://docs.rs#184)///
[185](https://docs.rs#185)/// A line terminator represents the end of a line. Generally, every line is
[186](https://docs.rs#186)/// either "terminated" by the end of a stream or a specific byte (or sequence
[187](https://docs.rs#187)/// of bytes).
[188](https://docs.rs#188)///
[189](https://docs.rs#189)/// Generally, a line terminator is a single byte, specifically, `\n`, on
[190](https://docs.rs#190)/// Unix-like systems. On Windows, a line terminator is `\r\n` (referred to
[191](https://docs.rs#191)/// as `CRLF` for `Carriage Return; Line Feed`).
[192](https://docs.rs#192)///
[193](https://docs.rs#193)/// The default line terminator is `\n` on all platforms.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Eq, Hash, PartialEq)]
[195](https://docs.rs#195)pub struct LineTerminator(LineTerminatorImp);
[196](https://docs.rs#196)
[197](https://docs.rs#197)#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, Eq, Hash, PartialEq)]
[198](https://docs.rs#198)enum LineTerminatorImp {
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    /// Any single byte representing a line terminator.
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    Byte(u8),
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    /// A line terminator represented by `\r\n`.
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    ///
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    /// When this option is used, consumers may generally treat a lone `\n` as
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    /// a line terminator in addition to `\r\n`.
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    CRLF,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)}
[207](https://docs.rs#207)
[208](https://docs.rs#208)impl LineTerminator {
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    /// Return a new single-byte line terminator. Any byte is valid.
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    #[inline]
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    pub fn byte(byte: u8) -> LineTerminator {
[212](https://docs.rs#212)        LineTerminator(LineTerminatorImp::Byte(byte))
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    }
[214](https://docs.rs#214)
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    /// Return a new line terminator represented by `\r\n`.
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    ///
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    /// When this option is used, consumers may generally treat a lone `\n` as
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    /// a line terminator in addition to `\r\n`.
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    #[inline]
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    pub fn crlf() -> LineTerminator {
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        LineTerminator(LineTerminatorImp::CRLF)
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    }
[223](https://docs.rs#223)
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// Returns true if and only if this line terminator is CRLF.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    #[inline]
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    pub fn is_crlf(&self) -> bool {
[227](https://docs.rs#227)        self.0 == LineTerminatorImp::CRLF
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    }
[229](https://docs.rs#229)
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    /// Returns this line terminator as a single byte.
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    ///
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// If the line terminator is CRLF, then this returns `\n`. This is
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    /// useful for routines that, for example, find line boundaries by treating
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    /// `\n` as a line terminator even when it isn't preceded by `\r`.
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    #[inline]
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    pub fn as_byte(&self) -> u8 {
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        match self.0 {
[238](https://docs.rs#238)            LineTerminatorImp::Byte(byte) => byte,
[239](https://docs.rs#239)            LineTerminatorImp::CRLF => b'\n',
[240](https://docs.rs#240)        }
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    }
[242](https://docs.rs#242)
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    /// Returns this line terminator as a sequence of bytes.
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    ///
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    /// This returns a singleton sequence for all line terminators except for
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// `CRLF`, in which case, it returns `\r\n`.
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    ///
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    /// The slice returned is guaranteed to have length at least `1`.
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    #[inline]
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    pub fn as_bytes(&self) -> &[u8] {
[251](https://docs.rs#251)        match self.0 {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)            LineTerminatorImp::Byte(ref byte) => std::slice::from_ref(byte),
[253](https://docs.rs#253)            LineTerminatorImp::CRLF => &[b'\r', b'\n'],
[254](https://docs.rs#254)        }
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    }
[256](https://docs.rs#256)
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// Returns true if and only if the given slice ends with this line
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    /// terminator.
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    ///
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    /// If this line terminator is `CRLF`, then this only checks whether the
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// last byte is `\n`.
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    #[inline]
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    pub fn is_suffix(&self, slice: &[u8]) -> bool {
[264](https://docs.rs#264)        slice.last().map_or(false, |&b| b == self.as_byte())
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    }

[275](https://docs.rs#275)/// A set of bytes.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)///
[277](https://docs.rs#277)/// In this crate, byte sets are used to express bytes that can never appear
[278](https://docs.rs#278)/// anywhere in a match for a particular implementation of the `Matcher` trait.
[279](https://docs.rs#279)/// Specifically, if such a set can be determined, then it's possible for
[280](https://docs.rs#280)/// callers to perform additional operations on the basis that certain bytes
[281](https://docs.rs#281)/// may never match.
[282](https://docs.rs#282)///
[283](https://docs.rs#283)/// For example, if a search is configured to possibly produce results that
[284](https://docs.rs#284)/// span multiple lines but a caller provided pattern can never match across
[285](https://docs.rs#285)/// multiple lines, then it may make sense to divert to more optimized line
[286](https://docs.rs#286)/// oriented routines that don't need to handle the multi-line match case.
[287](https://docs.rs#287)#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
[288](https://docs.rs#288)pub struct ByteSet(BitSet);
[289](https://docs.rs#289)
[290](https://docs.rs#290)#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
[291](https://docs.rs#291)struct BitSet([u64; 4]);
[292](https://docs.rs#292)
[293](https://docs.rs#293)impl std::fmt::Debug for BitSet {
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut std::fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> std::fmt::Result {
[295](https://docs.rs#295)        let mut fmtd = f.debug_set();
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        for b in 0..=255 {
[297](https://docs.rs#297)            if ByteSet(*self).contains(b) {
[298](https://docs.rs#298)                fmtd.entry(&b);
[299](https://docs.rs#299)            }
[300](https://docs.rs#300)        }
[301](https://docs.rs#301)        fmtd.finish()
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    }
[303](https://docs.rs#303)}
[304](https://docs.rs#304)
[305](https://docs.rs#305)impl ByteSet {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    /// Create an empty set of bytes.
[307](https://docs.rs#307)    #[inline]
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    pub fn empty() -> ByteSet {
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        ByteSet(BitSet([0; 4]))
[310](https://docs.rs#310)    }
[311](https://docs.rs#311)
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    /// Create a full set of bytes such that every possible byte is in the set
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    /// returned.
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    #[inline]
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    pub fn full() -> ByteSet {
[316](https://docs.rs#316)        ByteSet(BitSet([u64::MAX; 4]))
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    }
[318](https://docs.rs#318)
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    /// Add a byte to this set.
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    ///
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    /// If the given byte already belongs to this set, then this is a no-op.
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    #[inline]
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    pub fn add(&mut self, byte: u8) {
[324](https://docs.rs#324)        let bucket = byte / 64;
[325](https://docs.rs#325)        let bit = byte % 64;
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        (self.0).0[usize::from(bucket)] |= 1 << bit;
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    }
[328](https://docs.rs#328)
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    /// Add an inclusive range of bytes.
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    #[inline]
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    pub fn add_all(&mut self, start: u8, end: u8) {
[332](https://docs.rs#332)        for b in start..=end {
[333](https://docs.rs#333)            self.add(b);
[334](https://docs.rs#334)        }
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    }
[336](https://docs.rs#336)
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    /// Remove a byte from this set.
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    ///
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    /// If the given byte is not in this set, then this is a no-op.
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    #[inline]
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    pub fn remove(&mut self, byte: u8) {
[342](https://docs.rs#342)        let bucket = byte / 64;
[343](https://docs.rs#343)        let bit = byte % 64;
[344](https://docs.rs#344)        (self.0).0[usize::from(bucket)] &= !(1 << bit);
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    }
[346](https://docs.rs#346)
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    /// Remove an inclusive range of bytes.
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    #[inline]
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    pub fn remove_all(&mut self, start: u8, end: u8) {
[350](https://docs.rs#350)        for b in start..=end {
[351](https://docs.rs#351)            self.remove(b);
[352](https://docs.rs#352)        }
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    }
[354](https://docs.rs#354)
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    /// Return true if and only if the given byte is in this set.
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    #[inline]
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    pub fn contains(&self, byte: u8) -> bool {
[358](https://docs.rs#358)        let bucket = byte / 64;
[359](https://docs.rs#359)        let bit = byte % 64;
[360](https://docs.rs#360)        (self.0).0[usize::from(bucket)] & (1 << bit) > 0
[361](https://docs.rs#361)    }
[362](https://docs.rs#362)}
[363](https://docs.rs#363)
[364](https://docs.rs#364)/// A trait that describes implementations of capturing groups.
[365](https://docs.rs#365)///
[366](https://docs.rs#366)/// When a matcher supports capturing group extraction, then it is the
[367](https://docs.rs#367)/// matcher's responsibility to provide an implementation of this trait.
[368](https://docs.rs#368)///
[369](https://docs.rs#369)/// Principally, this trait provides a way to access capturing groups
[370](https://docs.rs#370)/// in a uniform way that does not require any specific representation.
[371](https://docs.rs#371)/// Namely, different matcher implementations may require different in-memory
[372](https://docs.rs#372)/// representations of capturing groups. This trait permits matchers to
[373](https://docs.rs#373)/// maintain their specific in-memory representation.
[374](https://docs.rs#374)///
[375](https://docs.rs#375)/// Note that this trait explicitly does not provide a way to construct a new
[376](https://docs.rs#376)/// capture value. Instead, it is the responsibility of a `Matcher` to build
[377](https://docs.rs#377)/// one, which might require knowledge of the matcher's internal implementation
[378](https://docs.rs#378)/// details.
[379](https://docs.rs#379)pub trait Captures {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// Return the total number of capturing groups. This includes capturing
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    /// groups that have not matched anything.
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    fn len(&self) -> usize;
[383](https://docs.rs#383)
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    /// Return the capturing group match at the given index. If no match of
[385](https://docs.rs#385)    /// that capturing group exists, then this returns `None`.
[386](https://docs.rs#386)    ///
[387](https://docs.rs#387)    /// When a matcher reports a match with capturing groups, then the first
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    /// capturing group (at index `0`) must always correspond to the offsets
[389](https://docs.rs#389)    /// for the overall match.
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    fn get(&self, i: usize) -> Option<Match>;
[391](https://docs.rs#391)
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    /// Return the overall match for the capture.
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    ///
[394](https://docs.rs#394)    /// This returns the match for index `0`. That is it is equivalent to
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    /// `get(0).unwrap()`
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    #[inline]
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    fn as_match(&self) -> Match {
[398](https://docs.rs#398)        self.get(0).unwrap()
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    }
[400](https://docs.rs#400)
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// Returns true if and only if these captures are empty. This occurs
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    /// when `len` is `0`.
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    ///
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    /// Note that capturing groups that have non-zero length but otherwise
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    /// contain no matching groups are *not* empty.
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    #[inline]
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
[408](https://docs.rs#408)        self.len() == 0
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    }
[410](https://docs.rs#410)
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    /// Expands all instances of `$name` in `replacement` to the corresponding
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    /// capture group `name`, and writes them to the `dst` buffer given.
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    ///
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    /// (Note: If you're looking for a convenient way to perform replacements
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    /// with interpolation, then you'll want to use the `replace_with_captures`
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// method on the `Matcher` trait.)
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    ///
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    /// `name` may be an integer corresponding to the index of the
[419](https://docs.rs#419)    /// capture group (counted by order of opening parenthesis where `0` is the
[420](https://docs.rs#420)    /// entire match) or it can be a name (consisting of letters, digits or
[421](https://docs.rs#421)    /// underscores) corresponding to a named capture group.
[422](https://docs.rs#422)    ///
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    /// A `name` is translated to a capture group index via the given
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    /// `name_to_index` function. If `name` isn't a valid capture group
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    /// (whether the name doesn't exist or isn't a valid index), then it is
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// replaced with the empty string.
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    ///
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// The longest possible name is used. e.g., `$1a` looks up the capture
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    /// group named `1a` and not the capture group at index `1`. To exert
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// more precise control over the name, use braces, e.g., `${1}a`. In all
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    /// cases, capture group names are limited to ASCII letters, numbers and
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// underscores.
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    ///
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    /// To write a literal `$` use `$$`.
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    ///
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// Note that the capture group match indices are resolved by slicing
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// the given `haystack`. Generally, this means that `haystack` should be
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// the same slice that was searched to get the current capture group
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// matches.
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    #[inline]
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    fn interpolate<F>(
[442](https://docs.rs#442)        &self,
[443](https://docs.rs#443)        name_to_index: F,
[444](https://docs.rs#444)        haystack: &[u8],
[445](https://docs.rs#445)        replacement: &[u8],
[446](https://docs.rs#446)        dst: &mut Vec<u8>,
[447](https://docs.rs#447)    ) where
[448](https://docs.rs#448)        F: FnMut(&str) -> Option<usize>,
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    {
[450](https://docs.rs#450)        interpolate(
[451](https://docs.rs#451)            replacement,
[452](https://docs.rs#452)            |i, dst| {
[453](https://docs.rs#453)                if let Some(range) = self.get(i) {
[454](https://docs.rs#454)                    dst.extend(&haystack[range]);
[455](https://docs.rs#455)                }
[456](https://docs.rs#456)            },
[457](https://docs.rs#457)            name_to_index,
[458](https://docs.rs#458)            dst,
[459](https://docs.rs#459)        )
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    }
[461](https://docs.rs#461)}
[462](https://docs.rs#462)

[517](https://docs.rs#517)/// The type of match for a line oriented matcher.

[519](https://docs.rs#519)pub enum LineMatchKind {

[532](https://docs.rs#532)
[533](https://docs.rs#533)/// A matcher defines an interface for regular expression implementations.
[534](https://docs.rs#534)///
[535](https://docs.rs#535)/// While this trait is large, there are only two required methods that
[536](https://docs.rs#536)/// implementors must provide: `find_at` and `new_captures`. If captures aren't
[537](https://docs.rs#537)/// supported by your implementation, then `new_captures` can be implemented
[538](https://docs.rs#538)/// with [`NoCaptures`]. If your implementation does support capture groups,
[539](https://docs.rs#539)/// then you should also implement the other capture related methods, as
[540](https://docs.rs#540)/// dictated by the documentation. Crucially, this includes `captures_at`.
[541](https://docs.rs#541)///
[542](https://docs.rs#542)/// The rest of the methods on this trait provide default implementations on
[543](https://docs.rs#543)/// top of `find_at` and `new_captures`. It is not uncommon for implementations
[544](https://docs.rs#544)/// to be able to provide faster variants of some methods; in those cases,
[545](https://docs.rs#545)/// simply override the default implementation.
[546](https://docs.rs#546)pub trait Matcher {
[547](https://docs.rs#547)    /// The concrete type of capturing groups used for this matcher.
[548](https://docs.rs#548)    ///
[549](https://docs.rs#549)    /// If this implementation does not support capturing groups, then set
[550](https://docs.rs#550)    /// this to `NoCaptures`.
[551](https://docs.rs#551)    type Captures: Captures;
[552](https://docs.rs#552)
[553](https://docs.rs#553)    /// The error type used by this matcher.
[554](https://docs.rs#554)    ///
[555](https://docs.rs#555)    /// For matchers in which an error is not possible, they are encouraged to
[556](https://docs.rs#556)    /// use the `NoError` type in this crate. In the future, when the "never"
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    /// (spelled `!`) type is stabilized, then it should probably be used
[558](https://docs.rs#558)    /// instead.
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    type Error: std::fmt::Display;
[560](https://docs.rs#560)
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    /// Returns the start and end byte range of the first match in `haystack`
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    /// after `at`, where the byte offsets are relative to that start of
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    /// `haystack` (and not `at`). If no match exists, then `None` is returned.
[564](https://docs.rs#564)    ///
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    /// The text encoding of `haystack` is not strictly specified. Matchers are
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    /// advised to assume UTF-8, or at worst, some ASCII compatible encoding.
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    ///
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    /// The significance of the starting point is that it takes the surrounding
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    /// context into consideration. For example, the `\A` anchor can only
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    /// match when `at == 0`.
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    fn find_at(
[572](https://docs.rs#572)        &self,
[573](https://docs.rs#573)        haystack: &[u8],
[574](https://docs.rs#574)        at: usize,
[575](https://docs.rs#575)    ) -> Result<Option<Match>, Self::Error>;
[576](https://docs.rs#576)
[577](https://docs.rs#577)    /// Creates an empty group of captures suitable for use with the capturing
[578](https://docs.rs#578)    /// APIs of this trait.
[579](https://docs.rs#579)    ///
[580](https://docs.rs#580)    /// Implementations that don't support capturing groups should use
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    /// the `NoCaptures` type and implement this method by calling
[582](https://docs.rs#582)    /// `NoCaptures::new()`.
[583](https://docs.rs#583)    fn new_captures(&self) -> Result<Self::Captures, Self::Error>;
[584](https://docs.rs#584)
[585](https://docs.rs#585)    /// Returns the total number of capturing groups in this matcher.
[586](https://docs.rs#586)    ///
[587](https://docs.rs#587)    /// If a matcher supports capturing groups, then this value must always be
[588](https://docs.rs#588)    /// at least 1, where the first capturing group always corresponds to the
[589](https://docs.rs#589)    /// overall match.
[590](https://docs.rs#590)    ///
[591](https://docs.rs#591)    /// If a matcher does not support capturing groups, then this should
[592](https://docs.rs#592)    /// always return 0.
[593](https://docs.rs#593)    ///
[594](https://docs.rs#594)    /// By default, capturing groups are not supported, so this always
[595](https://docs.rs#595)    /// returns 0.
[596](https://docs.rs#596)    #[inline]
[597](https://docs.rs#597)    fn capture_count(&self) -> usize {
[598](https://docs.rs#598)        0
[599](https://docs.rs#599)    }
[600](https://docs.rs#600)
[601](https://docs.rs#601)    /// Maps the given capture group name to its corresponding capture group
[602](https://docs.rs#602)    /// index, if one exists. If one does not exist, then `None` is returned.
[603](https://docs.rs#603)    ///
[604](https://docs.rs#604)    /// If the given capture group name maps to multiple indices, then it is
[605](https://docs.rs#605)    /// not specified which one is returned. However, it is guaranteed that
[606](https://docs.rs#606)    /// one of them is returned.
[607](https://docs.rs#607)    ///
[608](https://docs.rs#608)    /// By default, capturing groups are not supported, so this always returns
[609](https://docs.rs#609)    /// `None`.
[610](https://docs.rs#610)    #[inline]
[611](https://docs.rs#611)    fn capture_index(&self, _name: &str) -> Option<usize> {
[612](https://docs.rs#612)        None
[613](https://docs.rs#613)    }
[614](https://docs.rs#614)
[615](https://docs.rs#615)    /// Returns the start and end byte range of the first match in `haystack`.
[616](https://docs.rs#616)    /// If no match exists, then `None` is returned.
[617](https://docs.rs#617)    ///
[618](https://docs.rs#618)    /// The text encoding of `haystack` is not strictly specified. Matchers are
[619](https://docs.rs#619)    /// advised to assume UTF-8, or at worst, some ASCII compatible encoding.
[620](https://docs.rs#620)    #[inline]
[621](https://docs.rs#621)    fn find(&self, haystack: &[u8]) -> Result<Option<Match>, Self::Error> {
[622](https://docs.rs#622)        self.find_at(haystack, 0)
[623](https://docs.rs#623)    }
[624](https://docs.rs#624)
[625](https://docs.rs#625)    /// Executes the given function over successive non-overlapping matches
[626](https://docs.rs#626)    /// in `haystack`. If no match exists, then the given function is never
[627](https://docs.rs#627)    /// called. If the function returns `false`, then iteration stops.
[628](https://docs.rs#628)    #[inline]
[629](https://docs.rs#629)    fn find_iter<F>(
[630](https://docs.rs#630)        &self,
[631](https://docs.rs#631)        haystack: &[u8],
[632](https://docs.rs#632)        matched: F,
[633](https://docs.rs#633)    ) -> Result<(), Self::Error>
[634](https://docs.rs#634)    where
[635](https://docs.rs#635)        F: FnMut(Match) -> bool,
[636](https://docs.rs#636)    {
[637](https://docs.rs#637)        self.find_iter_at(haystack, 0, matched)
[638](https://docs.rs#638)    }
[639](https://docs.rs#639)
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    /// Executes the given function over successive non-overlapping matches
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    /// in `haystack`. If no match exists, then the given function is never
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    /// called. If the function returns `false`, then iteration stops.
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    ///
[644](https://docs.rs#644)    /// The significance of the starting point is that it takes the surrounding
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    /// context into consideration. For example, the `\A` anchor can only
[646](https://docs.rs#646)    /// match when `at == 0`.
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    #[inline]
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    fn find_iter_at<F>(

[661](https://docs.rs#661)    /// Executes the given function over successive non-overlapping matches
[662](https://docs.rs#662)    /// in `haystack`. If no match exists, then the given function is never
[663](https://docs.rs#663)    /// called. If the function returns `false`, then iteration stops.
[664](https://docs.rs#664)    /// Similarly, if the function returns an error then iteration stops and
[665](https://docs.rs#665)    /// the error is yielded. If an error occurs while executing the search,
[666](https://docs.rs#666)    /// then it is converted to
[667](https://docs.rs#667)    /// `E`.
[668](https://docs.rs#668)    #[inline]
[669](https://docs.rs#669)    fn try_find_iter<F, E>(
[670](https://docs.rs#670)        &self,
[671](https://docs.rs#671)        haystack: &[u8],
[672](https://docs.rs#672)        matched: F,
[673](https://docs.rs#673)    ) -> Result<Result<(), E>, Self::Error>
[674](https://docs.rs#674)    where
[675](https://docs.rs#675)        F: FnMut(Match) -> Result<bool, E>,
[676](https://docs.rs#676)    {
[677](https://docs.rs#677)        self.try_find_iter_at(haystack, 0, matched)
[678](https://docs.rs#678)    }
[679](https://docs.rs#679)
[680](https://docs.rs#680)    /// Executes the given function over successive non-overlapping matches
[681](https://docs.rs#681)    /// in `haystack`. If no match exists, then the given function is never
[682](https://docs.rs#682)    /// called. If the function returns `false`, then iteration stops.
[683](https://docs.rs#683)    /// Similarly, if the function returns an error then iteration stops and
[684](https://docs.rs#684)    /// the error is yielded. If an error occurs while executing the search,
[685](https://docs.rs#685)    /// then it is converted to
[686](https://docs.rs#686)    /// `E`.
[687](https://docs.rs#687)    ///
[688](https://docs.rs#688)    /// The significance of the starting point is that it takes the surrounding
[689](https://docs.rs#689)    /// context into consideration. For example, the `\A` anchor can only
[690](https://docs.rs#690)    /// match when `at == 0`.
[691](https://docs.rs#691)    #[inline]
[692](https://docs.rs#692)    fn try_find_iter_at<F, E>(
[693](https://docs.rs#693)        &self,
[694](https://docs.rs#694)        haystack: &[u8],
[695](https://docs.rs#695)        at: usize,
[696](https://docs.rs#696)        mut matched: F,
[697](https://docs.rs#697)    ) -> Result<Result<(), E>, Self::Error>
[698](https://docs.rs#698)    where
[699](https://docs.rs#699)        F: FnMut(Match) -> Result<bool, E>,
[700](https://docs.rs#700)    {
[701](https://docs.rs#701)        let mut last_end = at;
[702](https://docs.rs#702)        let mut last_match = None;
[703](https://docs.rs#703)
[704](https://docs.rs#704)        loop {
[705](https://docs.rs#705)            if last_end > haystack.len() {
[706](https://docs.rs#706)                return Ok(Ok(()));
[707](https://docs.rs#707)            }
[708](https://docs.rs#708)            let m = match self.find_at(haystack, last_end)? {
[709](https://docs.rs#709)                None => return Ok(Ok(())),
[710](https://docs.rs#710)                Some(m) => m,
[711](https://docs.rs#711)            };
[712](https://docs.rs#712)            if m.start == m.end {
[713](https://docs.rs#713)                // This is an empty match. To ensure we make progress, start
[714](https://docs.rs#714)                // the next search at the smallest possible starting position
[715](https://docs.rs#715)                // of the next match following this one.
[716](https://docs.rs#716)                last_end = m.end + 1;
[717](https://docs.rs#717)                // Don't accept empty matches immediately following a match.
[718](https://docs.rs#718)                // Just move on to the next match.
[719](https://docs.rs#719)                if Some(m.end) == last_match {
[720](https://docs.rs#720)                    continue;
[721](https://docs.rs#721)                }
[722](https://docs.rs#722)            } else {
[723](https://docs.rs#723)                last_end = m.end;
[724](https://docs.rs#724)            }
[725](https://docs.rs#725)            last_match = Some(m.end);
[726](https://docs.rs#726)            match matched(m) {
[727](https://docs.rs#727)                Ok(true) => continue,
[728](https://docs.rs#728)                Ok(false) => return Ok(Ok(())),
[729](https://docs.rs#729)                Err(err) => return Ok(Err(err)),
[730](https://docs.rs#730)            }
[731](https://docs.rs#731)        }
[732](https://docs.rs#732)    }
[733](https://docs.rs#733)
[734](https://docs.rs#734)    /// Populates the first set of capture group matches from `haystack` into
[735](https://docs.rs#735)    /// `caps`. If no match exists, then `false` is returned.
[736](https://docs.rs#736)    ///
[737](https://docs.rs#737)    /// The text encoding of `haystack` is not strictly specified. Matchers are
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    /// advised to assume UTF-8, or at worst, some ASCII compatible encoding.

[808](https://docs.rs#808)    /// Executes the given function over successive non-overlapping matches
[809](https://docs.rs#809)    /// in `haystack` with capture groups extracted from each match. If no
[810](https://docs.rs#810)    /// match exists, then the given function is never called. If the function
[811](https://docs.rs#811)    /// returns `false`, then iteration stops. Similarly, if the function
[812](https://docs.rs#812)    /// returns an error then iteration stops and the error is yielded. If
[813](https://docs.rs#813)    /// an error occurs while executing the search, then it is converted to
[814](https://docs.rs#814)    /// `E`.
[815](https://docs.rs#815)    ///
[816](https://docs.rs#816)    /// The significance of the starting point is that it takes the surrounding
[817](https://docs.rs#817)    /// context into consideration. For example, the `\A` anchor can only
[818](https://docs.rs#818)    /// match when `at == 0`.
[819](https://docs.rs#819)    #[inline]
[820](https://docs.rs#820)    fn try_captures_iter_at<F, E>(
[821](https://docs.rs#821)        &self,
[822](https://docs.rs#822)        haystack: &[u8],
[823](https://docs.rs#823)        at: usize,
[824](https://docs.rs#824)        caps: &mut Self::Captures,
[825](https://docs.rs#825)        mut matched: F,
[826](https://docs.rs#826)    ) -> Result<Result<(), E>, Self::Error>
[827](https://docs.rs#827)    where
[828](https://docs.rs#828)        F: FnMut(&Self::Captures) -> Result<bool, E>,
[829](https://docs.rs#829)    {
[830](https://docs.rs#830)        let mut last_end = at;
[831](https://docs.rs#831)        let mut last_match = None;
[832](https://docs.rs#832)
[833](https://docs.rs#833)        loop {
[834](https://docs.rs#834)            if last_end > haystack.len() {
[835](https://docs.rs#835)                return Ok(Ok(()));
[836](https://docs.rs#836)            }
[837](https://docs.rs#837)            if !self.captures_at(haystack, last_end, caps)? {
[838](https://docs.rs#838)                return Ok(Ok(()));
[839](https://docs.rs#839)            }
[840](https://docs.rs#840)            let m = caps.get(0).unwrap();
[841](https://docs.rs#841)            if m.start == m.end {
[842](https://docs.rs#842)                // This is an empty match. To ensure we make progress, start
[843](https://docs.rs#843)                // the next search at the smallest possible starting position
[844](https://docs.rs#844)                // of the next match following this one.
[845](https://docs.rs#845)                last_end = m.end + 1;
[846](https://docs.rs#846)                // Don't accept empty matches immediately following a match.
[847](https://docs.rs#847)                // Just move on to the next match.
[848](https://docs.rs#848)                if Some(m.end) == last_match {
[849](https://docs.rs#849)                    continue;
[850](https://docs.rs#850)                }
[851](https://docs.rs#851)            } else {
[852](https://docs.rs#852)                last_end = m.end;
[853](https://docs.rs#853)            }
[854](https://docs.rs#854)            last_match = Some(m.end);
[855](https://docs.rs#855)            match matched(caps) {
[856](https://docs.rs#856)                Ok(true) => continue,
[857](https://docs.rs#857)                Ok(false) => return Ok(Ok(())),
[858](https://docs.rs#858)                Err(err) => return Ok(Err(err)),
[859](https://docs.rs#859)            }
[860](https://docs.rs#860)        }
[861](https://docs.rs#861)    }
[862](https://docs.rs#862)
[863](https://docs.rs#863)    /// Populates the first set of capture group matches from `haystack`
[864](https://docs.rs#864)    /// into `matches` after `at`, where the byte offsets in each capturing
[865](https://docs.rs#865)    /// group are relative to the start of `haystack` (and not `at`). If no
[866](https://docs.rs#866)    /// match exists, then `false` is returned and the contents of the given
[867](https://docs.rs#867)    /// capturing groups are unspecified.
[868](https://docs.rs#868)    ///
[869](https://docs.rs#869)    /// The text encoding of `haystack` is not strictly specified. Matchers are
[870](https://docs.rs#870)    /// advised to assume UTF-8, or at worst, some ASCII compatible encoding.
[871](https://docs.rs#871)    ///
[872](https://docs.rs#872)    /// The significance of the starting point is that it takes the surrounding
[873](https://docs.rs#873)    /// context into consideration. For example, the `\A` anchor can only
[874](https://docs.rs#874)    /// match when `at == 0`.
[875](https://docs.rs#875)    ///
[876](https://docs.rs#876)    /// By default, capturing groups aren't supported, and this implementation
[877](https://docs.rs#877)    /// will always behave as if a match were impossible.
[878](https://docs.rs#878)    ///
[879](https://docs.rs#879)    /// Implementors that provide support for capturing groups must guarantee
[880](https://docs.rs#880)    /// that when a match occurs, the first capture match (at index `0`) is
[881](https://docs.rs#881)    /// always set to the overall match offsets.
[882](https://docs.rs#882)    ///
[883](https://docs.rs#883)    /// Note that if implementors seek to support capturing groups, then they
[884](https://docs.rs#884)    /// should implement this method. Other methods that match based on
[885](https://docs.rs#885)    /// captures will then work automatically.
[886](https://docs.rs#886)    #[inline]
[887](https://docs.rs#887)    fn captures_at(
[888](https://docs.rs#888)        &self,
[889](https://docs.rs#889)        _haystack: &[u8],
[890](https://docs.rs#890)        _at: usize,
[891](https://docs.rs#891)        _caps: &mut Self::Captures,
[892](https://docs.rs#892)    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
[893](https://docs.rs#893)        Ok(false)
[894](https://docs.rs#894)    }
[895](https://docs.rs#895)
[896](https://docs.rs#896)    /// Replaces every match in the given haystack with the result of calling
[897](https://docs.rs#897)    /// `append`. `append` is given the start and end of a match, along with
[898](https://docs.rs#898)    /// a handle to the `dst` buffer provided.
[899](https://docs.rs#899)    ///
[900](https://docs.rs#900)    /// If the given `append` function returns `false`, then replacement stops.
[901](https://docs.rs#901)    #[inline]
[902](https://docs.rs#902)    fn replace<F>(
[903](https://docs.rs#903)        &self,
[904](https://docs.rs#904)        haystack: &[u8],
[905](https://docs.rs#905)        dst: &mut Vec<u8>,
[906](https://docs.rs#906)        mut append: F,
[907](https://docs.rs#907)    ) -> Result<(), Self::Error>
[908](https://docs.rs#908)    where
[909](https://docs.rs#909)        F: FnMut(Match, &mut Vec<u8>) -> bool,
[910](https://docs.rs#910)    {
[911](https://docs.rs#911)        let mut last_match = 0;
[912](https://docs.rs#912)        self.find_iter(haystack, |m| {
[913](https://docs.rs#913)            dst.extend(&haystack[last_match..m.start]);
[914](https://docs.rs#914)            last_match = m.end;
[915](https://docs.rs#915)            append(m, dst)
[916](https://docs.rs#916)        })?;
[917](https://docs.rs#917)        dst.extend(&haystack[last_match..]);
[918](https://docs.rs#918)        Ok(())
[919](https://docs.rs#919)    }

[994](https://docs.rs#994)
[995](https://docs.rs#995)    /// Returns an end location of the first match in `haystack`. If no match
[996](https://docs.rs#996)    /// exists, then `None` is returned.
[997](https://docs.rs#997)    ///
[998](https://docs.rs#998)    /// Note that the end location reported by this method may be less than the
[999](https://docs.rs#999)    /// same end location reported by `find`. For example, running `find` with
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)    /// the pattern `a+` on the haystack `aaa` should report a range of `[0,
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)    /// 3)`, but `shortest_match` may report `1` as the ending location since
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)    /// that is the place at which a match is guaranteed to occur.
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)    ///
[1004](https://docs.rs#1004)    /// This method should never report false positives or false negatives. The
[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)    /// point of this method is that some implementors may be able to provide
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)    /// a faster implementation of this than what `find` does.
[1007](https://docs.rs#1007)    ///
[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)    /// By default, this method is implemented by calling `find`.
[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)    #[inline]
[1010](https://docs.rs#1010)    fn shortest_match(
[1011](https://docs.rs#1011)        &self,
[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)        haystack: &[u8],
[1013](https://docs.rs#1013)    ) -> Result<Option<usize>, Self::Error> {
[1014](https://docs.rs#1014)        self.shortest_match_at(haystack, 0)
[1015](https://docs.rs#1015)    }
[1016](https://docs.rs#1016)
[1017](https://docs.rs#1017)    /// Returns an end location of the first match in `haystack` starting at
[1018](https://docs.rs#1018)    /// the given position. If no match exists, then `None` is returned.
[1019](https://docs.rs#1019)    ///
[1020](https://docs.rs#1020)    /// Note that the end location reported by this method may be less than the
[1021](https://docs.rs#1021)    /// same end location reported by `find`. For example, running `find` with
[1022](https://docs.rs#1022)    /// the pattern `a+` on the haystack `aaa` should report a range of `[0,
[1023](https://docs.rs#1023)    /// 3)`, but `shortest_match` may report `1` as the ending location since
[1024](https://docs.rs#1024)    /// that is the place at which a match is guaranteed to occur.
[1025](https://docs.rs#1025)    ///
[1026](https://docs.rs#1026)    /// This method should never report false positives or false negatives. The
[1027](https://docs.rs#1027)    /// point of this method is that some implementors may be able to provide
[1028](https://docs.rs#1028)    /// a faster implementation of this than what `find` does.
[1029](https://docs.rs#1029)    ///
[1030](https://docs.rs#1030)    /// By default, this method is implemented by calling `find_at`.
[1031](https://docs.rs#1031)    ///
[1032](https://docs.rs#1032)    /// The significance of the starting point is that it takes the surrounding
[1033](https://docs.rs#1033)    /// context into consideration. For example, the `\A` anchor can only
[1034](https://docs.rs#1034)    /// match when `at == 0`.
[1035](https://docs.rs#1035)    #[inline]
[1036](https://docs.rs#1036)    fn shortest_match_at(
[1037](https://docs.rs#1037)        &self,
[1038](https://docs.rs#1038)        haystack: &[u8],
[1039](https://docs.rs#1039)        at: usize,
[1040](https://docs.rs#1040)    ) -> Result<Option<usize>, Self::Error> {
[1041](https://docs.rs#1041)        Ok(self.find_at(haystack, at)?.map(|m| m.end))
[1042](https://docs.rs#1042)    }
[1043](https://docs.rs#1043)
[1044](https://docs.rs#1044)    /// If available, return a set of bytes that will never appear in a match
[1045](https://docs.rs#1045)    /// produced by an implementation.
[1046](https://docs.rs#1046)    ///
[1047](https://docs.rs#1047)    /// Specifically, if such a set can be determined, then it's possible for
[1048](https://docs.rs#1048)    /// callers to perform additional operations on the basis that certain
[1049](https://docs.rs#1049)    /// bytes may never match.
[1050](https://docs.rs#1050)    ///
[1051](https://docs.rs#1051)    /// For example, if a search is configured to possibly produce results
[1052](https://docs.rs#1052)    /// that span multiple lines but a caller provided pattern can never
[1053](https://docs.rs#1053)    /// match across multiple lines, then it may make sense to divert to
[1054](https://docs.rs#1054)    /// more optimized line oriented routines that don't need to handle the
[1055](https://docs.rs#1055)    /// multi-line match case.
[1056](https://docs.rs#1056)    ///
[1057](https://docs.rs#1057)    /// Implementations that produce this set must never report false
[1058](https://docs.rs#1058)    /// positives, but may produce false negatives. That is, is a byte is in
[1059](https://docs.rs#1059)    /// this set then it must be guaranteed that it is never in a match. But,
[1060](https://docs.rs#1060)    /// if a byte is not in this set, then callers cannot assume that a match
[1061](https://docs.rs#1061)    /// exists with that byte.
[1062](https://docs.rs#1062)    ///
[1063](https://docs.rs#1063)    /// By default, this returns `None`.
[1064](https://docs.rs#1064)    #[inline]
[1065](https://docs.rs#1065)    fn non_matching_bytes(&self) -> Option<&ByteSet> {
[1066](https://docs.rs#1066)        None
[1067](https://docs.rs#1067)    }
[1068](https://docs.rs#1068)
[1069](https://docs.rs#1069)    /// If this matcher was compiled as a line oriented matcher, then this
[1070](https://docs.rs#1070)    /// method returns the line terminator if and only if the line terminator
[1071](https://docs.rs#1071)    /// never appears in any match produced by this matcher. If this wasn't
[1072](https://docs.rs#1072)    /// compiled as a line oriented matcher, or if the aforementioned guarantee
[1073](https://docs.rs#1073)    /// cannot be made, then this must return `None`, which is the default.
[1074](https://docs.rs#1074)    /// It is **never wrong** to return `None`, but returning a line terminator
[1075](https://docs.rs#1075)    /// when it can appear in a match results in unspecified behavior.
[1076](https://docs.rs#1076)    ///
[1077](https://docs.rs#1077)    /// The line terminator is typically `b'\n'`, but can be any single byte or
[1078](https://docs.rs#1078)    /// `CRLF`.
[1079](https://docs.rs#1079)    ///
[1080](https://docs.rs#1080)    /// By default, this returns `None`.
[1081](https://docs.rs#1081)    #[inline]
[1082](https://docs.rs#1082)    fn line_terminator(&self) -> Option<LineTerminator> {
[1083](https://docs.rs#1083)        None
[1084](https://docs.rs#1084)    }
[1085](https://docs.rs#1085)
[1086](https://docs.rs#1086)    /// Return one of the following: a confirmed line match, a candidate line
[1087](https://docs.rs#1087)    /// match (which may be a false positive) or no match at all (which **must
[1088](https://docs.rs#1088)    /// not** be a false negative). When reporting a confirmed or candidate
[1089](https://docs.rs#1089)    /// match, the position returned can be any position in the line.
[1090](https://docs.rs#1090)    ///
[1091](https://docs.rs#1091)    /// By default, this never returns a candidate match, and always either
[1092](https://docs.rs#1092)    /// returns a confirmed match or no match at all.
[1093](https://docs.rs#1093)    ///
[1094](https://docs.rs#1094)    /// When a matcher can match spans over multiple lines, then the behavior
[1095](https://docs.rs#1095)    /// of this method is unspecified. Namely, use of this method only
[1096](https://docs.rs#1096)    /// makes sense in a context where the caller is looking for the next
[1097](https://docs.rs#1097)    /// matching line. That is, callers should only use this method when
[1098](https://docs.rs#1098)    /// `line_terminator` does not return `None`.
[1099](https://docs.rs#1099)    ///
[1100](https://docs.rs#1100)    /// # Design rationale
[1101](https://docs.rs#1101)    ///
[1102](https://docs.rs#1102)    /// A line matcher is, fundamentally, a normal matcher with the addition
[1103](https://docs.rs#1103)    /// of one optional method: finding a line. By default, this routine
[1104](https://docs.rs#1104)    /// is implemented via the matcher's `shortest_match` method, which
[1105](https://docs.rs#1105)    /// always yields either no match or a `LineMatchKind::Confirmed`. However,
[1106](https://docs.rs#1106)    /// implementors may provide a routine for this that can return candidate
[1107](https://docs.rs#1107)    /// lines that need subsequent verification to be confirmed as a match.
[1108](https://docs.rs#1108)    /// This can be useful in cases where it may be quicker to find candidate
[1109](https://docs.rs#1109)    /// lines via some other means instead of relying on the more general
[1110](https://docs.rs#1110)    /// implementations for `find` and `shortest_match`.
[1111](https://docs.rs#1111)    ///
[1112](https://docs.rs#1112)    /// For example, consider the regex `\w+foo\s+`. Both `find` and
[1113](https://docs.rs#1113)    /// `shortest_match` must consider the entire regex, including the `\w+`
[1114](https://docs.rs#1114)    /// and `\s+`, while searching. However, this method could look for lines
[1115](https://docs.rs#1115)    /// containing `foo` and return them as candidates. Finding `foo` might
[1116](https://docs.rs#1116)    /// be implemented as a highly optimized substring search routine (like
[1117](https://docs.rs#1117)    /// `memmem`), which is likely to be faster than whatever more generalized
[1118](https://docs.rs#1118)    /// routine is required for resolving `\w+foo\s+`. The caller is then
[1119](https://docs.rs#1119)    /// responsible for confirming whether a match exists or not.
[1120](https://docs.rs#1120)    ///
[1121](https://docs.rs#1121)    /// Note that while this method may report false positives, it must never
[1122](https://docs.rs#1122)    /// report false negatives. That is, it can never skip over lines that
[1123](https://docs.rs#1123)    /// contain a match.
[1124](https://docs.rs#1124)    #[inline]
[1125](https://docs.rs#1125)    fn find_candidate_line(
[1126](https://docs.rs#1126)        &self,
[1127](https://docs.rs#1127)        haystack: &[u8],
[1128](https://docs.rs#1128)    ) -> Result<Option<LineMatchKind>, Self::Error> {
[1129](https://docs.rs#1129)        Ok(self.shortest_match(haystack)?.map(LineMatchKind::Confirmed))
[1130](https://docs.rs#1130)    }
[1131](https://docs.rs#1131)}

}## Expand description

A matcher defines an interface for regular expression implementations.

While this trait is large, there are only two required methods that
implementors must provide: `find_at` and `new_captures`. If captures aren’t
supported by your implementation, then `new_captures` can be implemented
with [ NoCaptures](https://docs.rs/struct.NoCaptures.html). If your implementation does support capture groups,
then you should also implement the other capture related methods, as
dictated by the documentation. Crucially, this includes

`captures_at`.The rest of the methods on this trait provide default implementations on
top of `find_at` and `new_captures`. It is not uncommon for implementations
to be able to provide faster variants of some methods; in those cases,
simply override the default implementation.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Returns the start and end byte range of the first match in `haystack`
after `at`, where the byte offsets are relative to that start of
`haystack` (and not `at`). If no match exists, then `None` is returned.

The text encoding of `haystack` is not strictly specified. Matchers are
advised to assume UTF-8, or at worst, some ASCII compatible encoding.

The significance of the starting point is that it takes the surrounding
context into consideration. For example, the `\A` anchor can only
match when `at == 0`.

#### fn [new_captures](https://docs.rs#tymethod.new_captures)(&self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self::[Captures](https://docs.rs/trait.Matcher.html#associatedtype.Captures), Self::[Error](https://docs.rs/trait.Matcher.html#associatedtype.Error)>

Creates an empty group of captures suitable for use with the capturing APIs of this trait.

Implementations that don’t support capturing groups should use
the `NoCaptures` type and implement this method by calling
`NoCaptures::new()`.

#### fn [capture_count](https://docs.rs#method.capture_count)(&self) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

Returns the total number of capturing groups in this matcher.

If a matcher supports capturing groups, then this value must always be at least 1, where the first capturing group always corresponds to the overall match.

If a matcher does not support capturing groups, then this should always return 0.

By default, capturing groups are not supported, so this always returns 0.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/grep_matcher/lib.rs.html#611-613)#### fn [capture_index](https://docs.rs#method.capture_index)(&self, _name: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/grep_matcher/lib.rs.html#611-613)

#### fn [capture_index](https://docs.rs#method.capture_index)(&self, _name: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)>

Maps the given capture group name to its corresponding capture group
index, if one exists. If one does not exist, then `None` is returned.

If the given capture group name maps to multiple indices, then it is not specified which one is returned. However, it is guaranteed that one of them is returned.

By default, capturing groups are not supported, so this always returns
`None`.

Returns the start and end byte range of the first match in `haystack`.
If no match exists, then `None` is returned.

The text encoding of `haystack` is not strictly specified. Matchers are
advised to assume UTF-8, or at worst, some ASCII compatible encoding.

Executes the given function over successive non-overlapping matches
in `haystack`. If no match exists, then the given function is never
called. If the function returns `false`, then iteration stops.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/grep_matcher/lib.rs.html#648-659)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/grep_matcher/lib.rs.html#648-659)

Executes the given function over successive non-overlapping matches
in `haystack`. If no match exists, then the given function is never
called. If the function returns `false`, then iteration stops.

The significance of the starting point is that it takes the surrounding
context into consideration. For example, the `\A` anchor can only
match when `at == 0`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/grep_matcher/lib.rs.html#669-678)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/grep_matcher/lib.rs.html#669-678)

Executes the given function over successive non-overlapping matches
in `haystack`. If no match exists, then the given function is never
called. If the function returns `false`, then iteration stops.
Similarly, if the function returns an error then iteration stops and
the error is yielded. If an error occurs while executing the search,
then it is converted to
`E`.

Executes the given function over successive non-overlapping matches
in `haystack`. If no match exists, then the given function is never
called. If the function returns `false`, then iteration stops.
Similarly, if the function returns an error then iteration stops and
the error is yielded. If an error occurs while executing the search,
then it is converted to
`E`.

The significance of the starting point is that it takes the surrounding
context into consideration. For example, the `\A` anchor can only
match when `at == 0`.

Populates the first set of capture group matches from `haystack`
into `matches` after `at`, where the byte offsets in each capturing
group are relative to the start of `haystack` (and not `at`). If no
match exists, then `false` is returned and the contents of the given
capturing groups are unspecified.

The text encoding of `haystack` is not strictly specified. Matchers are
advised to assume UTF-8, or at worst, some ASCII compatible encoding.

The significance of the starting point is that it takes the surrounding
context into consideration. For example, the `\A` anchor can only
match when `at == 0`.

By default, capturing groups aren’t supported, and this implementation will always behave as if a match were impossible.

Implementors that provide support for capturing groups must guarantee
that when a match occurs, the first capture match (at index `0`) is
always set to the overall match offsets.

Note that if implementors seek to support capturing groups, then they should implement this method. Other methods that match based on captures will then work automatically.

Returns true if and only if the matcher matches the given haystack.

By default, this method is implemented by calling `shortest_match`.

Returns true if and only if the matcher matches the given haystack starting at the given position.

By default, this method is implemented by calling `shortest_match_at`.

context into consideration. For example, the `\A` anchor can only
match when `at == 0`.

Returns an end location of the first match in `haystack`. If no match
exists, then `None` is returned.

Note that the end location reported by this method may be less than the
same end location reported by `find`. For example, running `find` with
the pattern `a+` on the haystack `aaa` should report a range of `[0, 3)`, but `shortest_match` may report `1` as the ending location since
that is the place at which a match is guaranteed to occur.

This method should never report false positives or false negatives. The
point of this method is that some implementors may be able to provide
a faster implementation of this than what `find` does.

By default, this method is implemented by calling `find`.
